theme: God is our refuge and strength
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 46 aloud. It is a psalm of the Sons of Korah, and it was the inspiration for Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress.” Read it three times: first for the images of chaos, second for the images of the city of God, and third for the repeated refrain, “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.”
settingTheScene: After the sobering opening of Judges, with its picture of a nation in decline, this psalm opens the week with a different note. It is about security in the middle of chaos. The psalm sets the shaking of the earth, the roaring of the seas, and the raging of nations against one unshakable fact: God is with his people. It was likely sung in Jerusalem, perhaps after a deliverance such as Sennacherib’s defeat. Whatever its original setting, it makes a powerful companion to the book of Judges, where God’s people were constantly in crisis and God was constantly their refuge.
observation: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (v. 1).
“Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea” (v. 2).
The waters “roar and foam” and the mountains “tremble at its swelling” (v. 3).
“There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High” (v. 4).
“God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns” (v. 5).
“The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts” (v. 6).
The refrain: “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (vv. 7, 11).
“Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a bold claim: God is not just a refuge from trouble but a “very present help in trouble.” The Hebrew phrase suggests that he is readily found. You do not have to search for him. In the moment of crisis, he is there. The consequence follows at once: “Therefore we will not fear.” Fear is not removed by changing circumstances but by a deeper fact.

The first stanza uses the language of cosmic catastrophe. Mountains fall into the sea, and waters roar. In the ancient world, the sea was the symbol of chaos, and the mountains were the symbol of stability. The psalm imagines both of these being undone. If anything could shake a believer, it would be this. Yet the declaration is, “we will not fear.” The point is not that disasters never come, but that they cannot unseat the God who is present with us.

The second stanza turns to the city of God. There is a river whose streams make it glad. This is striking, because Jerusalem had no river. The psalm is describing something spiritual: the presence of God is the river that nourishes his people. It echoes Eden’s river in Genesis 2 and anticipates the river of the water of life in Revelation 22. In the midst of this city, God dwells. “She shall not be moved.” While the mountains shake, the city stays secure, because God is in her.

The third stanza shifts to the nations and the end of war. The LORD speaks, and the earth melts. He breaks the bow and burns the chariots. The psalm ends with a call: “Be still, and know that I am God.” This is not a gentle invitation to quiet meditation, though it can include that. In context, it is a command to the raging nations to cease their fighting. “Be still” means “stop” or “let go.” But it is also a word to God’s people. When we are anxious, we are told to cease striving and acknowledge God’s rule. The knowledge of God’s sovereignty is the antidote to panic.

The refrain, “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress,” ties together the great and the small. He is the commander of heaven’s armies, and he is the God of Jacob, the God who chose a flawed man and bound himself to him. This is the God who stands with Israel in the book of Judges, and with the church today. His name for us in the New Testament is Immanuel, “God with us.”
connection: The river echoes Genesis 2:10, Ezekiel 47, and Revelation 22:1-2. The deliverance of Jerusalem recalls Isaiah 36-37. The breaking of the bow is also promised in Hosea 2:18 and Zechariah 9:10. “The LORD of hosts is with us” prepares for Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23, “Immanuel.” Jesus stills the storm in Mark 4:35-41, which shows that he is the God of this psalm.
application:
Identify one area where fear has taken hold. Perhaps it is health, work, a family concern, or the news. Read verses 1-3 and say, “Therefore I will not fear.” Then speak the refrain aloud.

Practice stillness. Set a timer for five minutes today, and in silence, simply repeat “Be still, and know that I am God.” Notice what you are tempted to do instead.

Finally, praise God for his presence in the church. The city of God is not shaken, even when its members are. Thank him for the community he has given you.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you are afraid of, and speak Psalm 46:1 over it.
Ask him to quiet your striving and teach you to be still.
Thank him that in Christ he is with you.
